title: Choose class, struct or record semantics from identity, equality, copying and inheritance requirements

questions.prompt:
A printer queue entry represents one ongoing print job. Two jobs remain distinct even when all their current properties match. Several components hold the same entry, and cancellation through one component must be visible to the others.

Explain why an ordinary `class` fits these requirements better than a `struct` or a record with its generated equality.

rubric.point: Connects class reference identity to treating separate jobs as distinct despite matching property values.
Explains that assigning a class instance copies its reference, so components sharing that instance observe its mutations.
Explains that struct assignment copies the value, while generated record equality compares data rather than job identity.

questions.model: An ordinary class gives each job object its own identity, so separate instances remain distinct even when their properties match. Assignment copies the reference: components holding that reference observe cancellation on the same object. A struct would copy the entry's fields on assignment, so changing a copied cancellation field would not update the original. Generated record equality would treat matching job data as equal, which conflicts with the required identity semantics.

questions.prompt:
A `TileAddress` contains only two integers: row and column. It has no identity or inheritance requirements. Assignment should produce a separate value, and matching coordinates should work with `==` and as dictionary keys without handwritten equality code. Existing addresses should not be mutable after construction.

Explain why `readonly record struct` fits, including what `readonly` and `record` each contribute beyond a plain struct.

rubric.point: Explains that struct assignment copies the two integer fields into a separate value, matching the small, identity-free model.
Explains that record supplies generated value equality, equality operators and a compatible hash code.
Explains that readonly prevents later mutation of the instance's own state; positional properties are init-only.

questions.model: The struct form gives value-copy semantics: assignment copies the two integers, so each variable holds a separate address value. The value is small and needs no inheritance. `record` generates equality and hashing based on the coordinates, including `==`, so matching addresses compare equal and work as dictionary keys without handwritten equality members. `readonly` prevents later mutation of the instance's state; positional properties use `get`/`init` rather than `get`/`set`.

questions.prompt:
A reporting system models immutable report descriptions using an abstract base type and specialised derived types. Separately constructed descriptions of the same concrete type should compare equal when their stored data matches. A revised description should be created with `with`.

A teammate recommends `record struct` because “records provide value equality and copies.” Explain why a record-class hierarchy fits instead, and distinguish ordinary assignment from `with`. Would `with` also give an independent copy of a mutable object stored in a member?

rubric.point: Explains that record classes support the required abstract base and derived record hierarchy, whereas record structs cannot participate in that inheritance.
Explains that generated record-class equality compares stored data and accounts for runtime type.
Distinguishes assignment, which copies a reference to the same instance, from with, which creates a separate record instance with selected changes.
Explains that the generated with copy is shallow, so a referenced mutable object remains shared unless explicitly copied or replaced.

questions.model: An abstract record class can provide the base, with specialised record classes deriving from it. A record struct cannot form that inheritance hierarchy. Record classes still generate value equality: descriptions of the same runtime type compare their stored data, while different derived types do not become equal merely because their shared base data matches. Ordinary assignment copies a reference to the same description. `with` creates a separate record instance and applies the requested changes. Its generated copy is shallow, so a mutable object held in a member remains shared unless it is explicitly copied or replaced. Record syntax alone therefore does not guarantee deep immutability.
